claims.statement: OpenWiki bundle maintenance is split into a free, offline, keyless planning target (`pnpm nx wiki-plan infrastructure-as-code`, which decomposes documentation changes since the last recorded run into slices of at most 8 pages, each exactly one bundle area) and a paid execution target (`pnpm nx wiki-maintain infrastructure-as-code`) that needs the selected provider's credential; the run record lives at `openwiki/.maintenance-state.json`, committed because CI runners are ephemeral, and is distinct from the tool's own `openwiki/.last-update.json`. Besides `coveredCommit` it carries the `backlog`, the `escalations` tags a deadline stop writes, the `parked` entries that take a page out of planning, the open `proposal` pointer with the `markerBefore` a roll-back needs, `lastRunBudget`, and `lastRunUsage`/`lastRunInvocations`, so one committed file answers what is outstanding, tagged, parked, proposed and what the last run cost.

Which model writes the bundle is configuration rather than code: `scripts/wiki-provider.mjs` is the single table resolved in one pure place from `MCM_WIKI_PROVIDER`, with `anthropic`/`claude-sonnet-5` as the local default (unset) and `fireworks`/`accounts/fireworks/models/deepseek-v4p1-flash` as the CI default at page concurrency 4; any malformed value throws (exit 2) and is never read as a default, while an empty value counts as unset. The service tier and the reasoning effort are declared per provider row, so setting one on a provider that does not take it is an error rather than something quietly ignored, while page concurrency is validated against one 1-8 bound for every provider alike. The per-turn output cap is the same idea in the other direction: not an operator variable but a property of the row, which may only ever raise the target's 16384 floor (65536 on the Fireworks row, no raise on Anthropic).

The Nx `wiki-update` target deliberately names no provider or model, because Nx builds a target's child env as `{ ...process.env, ...targetEnv }` and a provider in the target's `env` would silently overwrite the job's choice; the target instead runs `scripts/wiki-generate.mjs`, which resolves the table, hands the generator only the selected provider's credential (every other provider's key is deleted from the child env, along with the selector knobs themselves), and passes `WIKI_RUN_MESSAGE` as a single argv element with no shell.

The workflow's first step records `WIKI_JOB_DEADLINE` (epoch seconds) from a window chosen per event: `workflow_dispatch` gets `DISPATCH_MINUTES=120`, pinned equal to the job's `timeout-minutes`, and `push` gets `PUSH_MINUTES=60`, so a merge-triggered run keeps the shared-runner hold and raising the ceiling cannot lengthen the runs every merge starts; the guard test asserts both values.

Each generator invocation runs under GNU `timeout --kill-after=60s` with the time left before the job deadline minus an 8-minute reserve (`DEADLINE_RESERVE_MS`, held back for verification, publishing and the run-record commit), and a slice with under 5 minutes of allowance (`MIN_GENERATOR_MS`) is not started at all but carried forward as a budget stop at exit 3; the allowance is recomputed per attempt so a retry is never started with under 5 minutes left either.

A deadline stop does not by itself fail a slice: after `revertUnrequested` restores what the slice did not request, the slice is judged on what landed like any other, and in practice a stopped generator leaves a requested page unwritten or stale, which fails the slice (exit 1) — while either way the run still commits its run record, usage and failure digest, so a hang is recorded rather than dying with the job; a malformed `WIKI_JOB_DEADLINE` is an error (exit 2) and is never ignored, and because only the workflow sets the variable an interactive local run is never wrapped.

`timeout` signals the whole process group, which is load-bearing because Nx spawns openwiki as a grandchild and a plain `spawnSync` timeout would kill only Nx and leave the generator writing into the tree being verified; this holds while Nx uses no pseudo-terminal, and Nx uses one only when stdout is a TTY, which never happens in CI (stdout is piped through `ci-log-step.sh`).

For an OpenAI-compatible provider such as Fireworks openwiki sets no request timeout, so the OpenAI SDK's 10-minute default applies, and at page concurrency above 1 openwiki retries 5 times — one model request accepted and never answered was about 60 silent minutes; the launcher now injects `OPENWIKI_PROVIDER_RETRY_ATTEMPTS=2` into the generator's environment unless an explicit operator value is already present, bounding that at roughly 30 minutes, and a merge-triggered run also spends its first 15 minutes in the debounce so it has about 45 minutes rather than 60.

Dispatched runs get the full 120-minute window because an uncovered page (no `.page-manifest.json` entry, left by openwiki for full review) needs about 1.65x the output per call and over 1.6x the calls of a covered one, Fireworks generation speed varies hourly (measured 45-145 tok/s), and at 70-80 tok/s a page stopped at the old 51-minute deadline after 93 calls of ~29.5s each; uncovered pages are therefore processed one per dispatched run by seeding `backlog` in `openwiki/.maintenance-state.json` through a pull request, merging it, and dispatching.

The budget constants live in `scripts/wiki-maintain.mjs` — `PAGE_BUDGET`/`MAX_PAGES_PER_INVOCATION` of 8 pages, `TIME_BUDGET_SECONDS` of 4 minutes as a deadline for *starting* work, `WORST_INVOCATION_SECONDS` of 30 minutes for two waves of page workers at concurrency 4 — and the guard test derives the workflow's `timeout-minutes` from them, asserting the value and at least 5 minutes of margin, so changing one without the other fails offline; neither budget is a monetary bound (the wall-clock budget bounds runner occupancy).

Exit codes are: 0 for a plan produced or every attempted slice verified or nothing to do; 1 for a slice that failed verification, a generator stopped at the job deadline, or work that could not be published (marker held, slices returned to the backlog); 2 for bad usage, an unreadable run record, a missing credential, a malformed `MCM_WIKI_*` value or `WIKI_JOB_DEADLINE`, a failed preflight or a policy file that will not load; and 3 for stopping with work outstanding — which is explicitly not a failure because the remainder is in the backlog.

A finished slice is judged by what actually landed in the working tree, and fails when any of five things is true — a requested page does not exist after the run (an `index.md`-only refresh counts as zero pages), the bundle stopped being conformant under `check-openwiki-okf.mjs` rules V1-V16 (V16 included, since breaking it stops every later run), a written path was not permitted by the regeneration policy, a requested page is still stale because its cited source's last git commit is newer than its stamp, or a requested page was left mid-edit by its worker and named by V16 — and the generator's own exit status is not one of them.

The stale-page cause is judged after the run whether or not the page was written (items #587 and #616), because 'written' only means the bytes changed: on proposal #615 a run deleted a `verified:` block, left the body and its `generated` stamp alone, the page counted as written, and a check that skipped written pages never examined it, so the marker advanced past the source change exactly as in #587. A real rewrite moves `generated.at` past the source's commit and is never flagged, and a page whose source has not moved since its stamp may honestly write nothing.

Only the page-attributable causes are attributable to particular pages of an invocation: `verifySlice` then reports `landedParts` and names the failed pages individually (`failedPages`), and `proposableSlices` proposes the verified invocations plus those landed parts while only the failed pages return to the backlog — judged per page rather than per part since item #720, measured on run 5010 (2026-10-10) where one `runbooks` page exited without submitting and the two completed pages beside it were restored and carried forward with it (about $2.26 for one page), and across areas on run 4399 where a landed `runbooks/backlog.md` was otherwise lost. A whole-invocation failure such as a policy violation proposes nothing, returns every page, and names every page as failed.

After a deadline stop the run restores every path it changed to its committed state (or deletes it if newly created) EXCEPT the requested pages, their `.claims` sidecars, the requested areas' `index.md`, and any unrequested page whose worker submitted before the stop — a submission being durable because openwiki 0.7.1 finalizes a page's Claims on `submit_page`, so its sidecar certifies its bytes with a `verification.at` no earlier than the invocation's start; paths that were dirty before the run are left alone. This exists because openwiki forces every page with a stale Claims issue into a run, so a generator killed part-way (GNU `timeout` exit 124 or 137) can leave a page it was never asked for half-written and break V16 — which on run 4606 discarded the requested page's paid regeneration.

The deadline-stop revert applies only when the generator was stopped by the deadline; a generator that exits on its own is judged on everything it wrote, so a broken unrequested page on a normal exit still fails the slice rather than being quietly reverted.

A slice is retried up to 3 times within one run before returning to the backlog, and the working tree is snapshotted once before the first attempt so a retry can never forgive what an earlier attempt did (re-snapshotting per attempt laundered a policy violation into a success); one usage log is shared across an invocation's retries, because a retry's tokens are real spend too.

The backlog is committed, so it outlives the policy that produced it, and is re-validated against the current policy on every plan — a slice that can never succeed is dropped and reported as `carried-forward page(s) dropped` rather than starving the queue — and a failed slice no longer blocks the next one, because the run stops only after two consecutive failures.

Claims sidecars live under `openwiki/.claims/`, one JSON file per page mirroring the page's path, and carry `schemaVersion`, a `pageVersion` hash, a `verification: {by, at}` event and a `claims` array whose entries each have a stable `id`, a `statement` and one or more `evidence` entries (`repo://<path>` optionally with `#Lx-Ly`, plus a resolver-computed version hash); on a later refresh a claim is marked `stale` when its evidence version no longer matches or `unresolved` when the evidence cannot be resolved, and the generator must confirm, revise or retract it.

`openwiki/.page-manifest.json` lists every page openwiki has covered, and V16 (implemented by `claimsDurabilityFindings` in `scripts/openwiki-claims.mjs`, the same check openwiki performs in `buildManifestEntry`) requires each covered page's sidecar to exist, carry a `verification`, and record a `pageVersion` equal to the sha256 of the page's current bytes; otherwise openwiki throws 'Markdown and verified Claims are not durable' and fails the whole run before any generation, which is why a hand edit of a covered page bricks every later run, and a pull request that does so now goes red at review time.

Uncovering a page is the escape hatch for correcting a covered page by hand: with no `.page-manifest.json` entry openwiki leaves the page for full review and V16 does not check it, so the correction is made by removing the manifest entry, deleting the sidecar and deleting the front-matter `verified:` event in the same commit; the same module's `carryClaimsHash` lets link normalization move a covered page's certified hash across a pure link rewrite, but only for a page that was durable before the rewrite, never laundering an already-broken one.

Nothing yet checks that a sidecar's claims are true — V16's durability check is the only gate on sidecars — so a sidecar records what the generator asserted about a page rather than reviewed content, and the operator's 2026-09-27 decision (item #513) is that Claims are required and valuable.

The proposal is one long-lived branch (`openwiki-maintenance`) carrying at most one open pull request ever, and it is never auto-merged; because the CI runner is a fresh checkout the branch exists only on the remote, so a run that finds the proposal open continues the *remote* branch, rebases it onto the base and appends, and the push refuses outright when `git cherry` shows a commit the open proposal holds that the new head lacks — a red run rather than a silent overwrite.

When the run record and the forge disagree about an open proposal the forge wins: the record's `proposal` pointer is a cache, so a run asks the forge which proposal is open for the branch before creating one, adopts it if found, and treats a 409 from `forge POST /pulls` as 'someone beat me to it — adopt and update' rather than a fatal error, which makes a run that lost its record self-healing. The adoption happens at reconcile, BEFORE planning, including when the record's own pointer has just been reconciled as merged or closed: run 5229's record pointed at a proposal merged in the same second as the merge that started it while another run had already opened a different one, so the run generated onto a fresh branch and the publish step correctly refused to push — after about $1.35 had been spent on four pages.

The CI run debounces with `concurrency` + `cancel-in-progress: true` plus an initial 15-minute sleep so a burst of merges produces exactly one run, but never defers past a git-derived 6-hour maximum deferral because the waiting run is cancelled and any in-memory timer dies with it; `workflow_dispatch` bypasses the wait entirely, and the run does not trigger itself (`[skip ci]` marker commit or a bundle-only change).

Closing a proposal without merging returns its work to the backlog and rolls the marker back, and both halves are fixed as of item #619 (2026-10-09): `executeRun` reconciles the previous proposal BEFORE it plans (so the returned slices are planned and the run's own backlog and marker cannot overwrite the reconciled ones), and `markerBefore` is the marker the opening run *found* — read before generation — rather than the one it advanced to, which would make the roll-back a no-op; reconciling is free, precedes the preflight, stops the run at exit 2 if the forge cannot be reached for it, and persists nothing under `--dry-run`.

When publishing itself fails (the push or the forge call), the marker is held and the run's slices go back to the backlog so nothing is certified that never reached a proposal, while the recorded usage stays because that money was already spent; the run exits 1.

The generator writes site-root-absolute body links (`](/openwiki/...)`) that are dead on this forge because a leading `/` resolves against the site root, and three layers hold the line: `openwiki/INSTRUCTIONS.md` §6 states the convention, `verifySlice` deterministically normalizes whatever the slice wrote before the OKF gate reads it, and `okf-lint` rules V14 (site-root-absolute) and V15 (does not resolve from its own file's directory) fail the build for anything arriving by another route; a bundle-wide sweep is `node scripts/wiki-maintain.mjs --normalize-links`, which is offline, needs no credential and skips code fences and code spans.

The page stamp is the newest of `generated.at`, `verified.at` and `timestamp`, resolved in exactly one place (`scripts/openwiki-stamp.mjs`, `conceptStamp`), which is imported by both the OKF gate's V12 drift check and wiki-maintain's `sourceNewerThanStamp` check so the two cannot disagree about which date a page carries; an older verification never drags a newer generation backwards, and the comparison is against the cited source's last git *commit* date, never its mtime.

V12 drift is warn-only and never touches the exit code, but since feature 082 it IS an input to the planner: every plan also looks for drifted concepts and plans up to `DRIFT_PAGES_PER_RUN` (2) of them per run, so a page that fell behind the marker is re-planned automatically rather than needing a hand-seeded sweep.

`mermaid` and `jsdom` are optional peer dependencies of the generator, and without them OpenWiki falls back to a weaker built-in diagram check that silently rewrites failing fences into plain `text` fences while the run still exits 0 and every gate still passes; both are therefore pinned beside the generator in `.devcontainer/toolchain.Dockerfile` and in `tools/openwiki-generator/package.json` (the locked install the wiki-maintain job uses), and a guard fails if either environment drops them or the two disagree about what a valid diagram is.

The per-turn output cap is load-bearing and set explicitly: the `wiki-update` target sets `OPENWIKI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=16384` rather than trusting OpenWiki's or the vendor SDK's own resolution, because a turn truncated at a too-small cap before it opens a `tool_use` block yields zero tool calls — LangGraph's ReAct stop condition — and the run exits 0 having written nothing; the guard test fails an unset or too-small cap, a model id OpenWiki's resolver does not match, and any id that would land on the 4096 fallback.

The generator's installed-version checks skip wherever the pinned generator is not installed — every guardrail job — and a skip misleadingly reads as a pass, so the wiki-maintain CI job (the one place it IS installed) runs the guard after installing the generator and before any paid work, pointing `OPENWIKI_ROOT` at the locked install and failing the step on a skip by reading node's `# skipped 0` TAP summary line.

The managed `<!-- OPENWIKI:START -->...<!-- OPENWIKI:END -->` block is rewritten in `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` on every run, and the regeneration policy permits only `actor: agent` to write `AGENTS.md`, so the committed block must already be byte-identical to what the pinned generator writes; the guard rebuilds both blocks from the installed generator's source and compares them byte-for-byte, so a version bump that changes the text fails offline instead of failing every paid slice.

A protected passage may only live on a concept that carries no `resource`, because freezing a derived summary against the document it summarizes would fail every legitimate refresh; changing such a passage requires updating its text and its fingerprint in the same change via `node scripts/check-openwiki-governance.mjs --fingerprint <concept> "<heading>"`, and the governance gate fails a refresh that silently rewords a load-bearing passage.

Remediation for a page that trips the conformance gate, a leak scan or the governance gate is always the brief — fix `openwiki/INSTRUCTIONS.md` and re-run — never an allowlist, because the gates deliberately have no skip flag and an allowlisted leak stays leaked.

A filename is not a specification: the run message carries a one-line subject per page, and measured across the feature-044 relocation that single change was the difference between 0 pages in 643s and 3 pages in 367s; the planner asks for at most 8 pages when refreshing existing concepts but only 3 when creating new ones (`MAX_NEW_PAGES_PER_SLICE`) and never mixes the two kinds in one slice, with the creation cap of 3 explicitly unverified because it was calibrated while every turn was silently capped at 4096 output tokens.

A usage tap (`scripts/wiki-usage-tap.mjs`) loaded into the generator process records per-call counts — never content — which are priced from the dated table `scripts/wiki-provider-prices.json` and reported in the job log and as `lastRunUsage` in the run record; the figure is an estimate, `not captured` is never written as $0, `PARTIAL total` means some invocations were not captured, `failedCalls` counts non-200 responses so rate limiting under page concurrency shows up there first, and when the reasoning effort is set the per-invocation and run lines carry `effort=<value>` and the record carries it in `reasoningEffort` without changing the price, because Fireworks bills reasoning tokens as output tokens.

Before the first paid slice, `wiki-maintain --execute` makes one minimal call to the selected model (`node scripts/wiki-generate.mjs --preflight` does the same by hand), and a failure exits 2 with the run record untouched and names the provider's error type, so a withdrawn model id, a revoked key or a blocked egress host costs one token rather than a slice.

Verification also normalizes body-link form only over the paths the current slice wrote, after those paths have cleared the policy check, because sweeping the whole bundle there would edit pages the slice never touched and no policy decision covered — the kind of unrequested write the verifier exists to catch.

The `--selftest` mode proves the planner and the verifier offline and keyless against fixtures plus a deliberately sabotaged generator that exits 0 having written nothing — the exact false green feature 043 measured — and the verifier must fail that zero-page slice, return it to the backlog, hold the marker, and still pass a slice that genuinely wrote its page, so a clean verdict there means the zero-page detector is broken. It is documented on the page under the 'Verifying the machinery itself' section, alongside the lint and governance gates (`pnpm nx okf-lint infrastructure-as-code`, `pnpm nx okf-governance infrastructure-as-code`) and the wiki-maintain and openwiki-links test files.

The generator is always invoked through the Nx target and never as a bare `openwiki` CLI, because the target carries `OPENWIKI_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1` and the raised Node heap — a bare call skips the telemetry opt-out and OOMs — and `wiki-maintain` shells out to `pnpm nx wiki-update infrastructure-as-code --output-style=stream` for exactly that reason, with the streaming output style putting the generator's own account of the run into the CI failure digest.

`MCM_WIKI_REASONING_EFFORT` (item #525) is a Fireworks-only knob accepting `none`, `low`, `high` or `max` (unset = the model's own default, which is `high` for this model), and `scripts/wiki-provider.mjs` throws for any value the provider does not document for this model or when the knob is set on a provider that takes none; because openwiki refuses an effort for its `fireworks` provider — true in 0.6.0 and still true in the pinned 0.7.1 (078 research R15) — the value cannot travel as `OPENWIKI_REASONING_EFFORT` and is instead set as `reasoning_effort` on the Fireworks chat-completions request bodies by the usage tap loaded into the generator process, the same route `MCM_WIKI_SERVICE_TIER` uses, with the preflight sending it too so a rejected value fails before any paid work.

In CI the reasoning effort is the `reasoning-effort` input of a **dispatched** run only: the job's `MCM_WIKI_REASONING_EFFORT` falls back to a repository variable that stays unset, so a trial never changes what a merge-triggered run sends — which is why the knob is described as under trial and the repository variable should not be set until a trial's page has been reviewed.

The ways a concept used to fall behind the run-record marker are tracked separately and are now all closed: **#526 (closed by feature 082)** is the general gap that nothing re-planned a concept once the marker had passed its source change, remedied by the bounded drift planner; **#587 (fixed)** is a refresh slice that wrote nothing for a requested page verifying as `noChange` and advancing the marker (measured on `openwiki/runbooks/renovate.md`, 2026-09-26), closed by `verifySlice` failing such a page when its source is newer than its stamp; **#616 (closed)** is the same gap through the front-matter-only door (proposal #615), whose two guards shipped in #617 and whose last route was closed by #685's restore of a failed page's page, sidecar and manifest entry; and **#525 (closed)** is the drift-driven sweep that cleared the 2026-09 V12 list once #587 was fixed and the canonical sources corrected (#588).

The generator pin is shared between the two environments and asserted by a guard: the dev container's `.devcontainer/toolchain.Dockerfile` and the locked install in `tools/openwiki-generator/` name the same `openwiki` version (0.7.1) plus the same `mermaid` and `jsdom` peers, and the guard reads the dev container's real install command line against the locked manifest and lockfile and fails if the versions or peer sets differ, because CI and a developer's container would otherwise silently differ on the thing whose output is gated. 0.6.0 was the first version with parallel page workers; the 2026-10-07 amendment moved the pin to 0.7.1, which adds the worker retry (upstream #913 — a page worker that exits without submitting is retried once with the page and its Claims restored, at the cost of up to two workers' time for a page that never submits) and scoped planning (upstream #865 — a run message naming pages is a hard mandate, though a page with a Claims issue is still forced into the run).

Only a deadline stop creates an escalation tag, and the test is the exit status rather than any openwiki text: a page is tagged when GNU `timeout` stopped its generator (exit 124, or 137 after `--kill-after`) with a deadline in force, while a worker that exited without submitting, a provider 429, an openwiki state error and a policy or conformance violation all end as normal exits and tag nothing, because `low` does not cure any of them (item #682); a start-deadline carry-forward — a slice never started because under 5 minutes were left — is not a failure either and does not tag.

Escalation tags live in `escalations` in `openwiki/.maintenance-state.json`, keyed `area/page` and stored beside the backlog rather than inside it so the committed backlog keeps its shape, each entry `{effort, reason: 'deadline', since, failuresAtLow}`; the run record's shape check rejects a non-object `escalations` or an entry without a string `effort` and a non-negative integer `failuresAtLow`.

Tagged pages are split out of the queue, packed among themselves and run at `reasoning_effort: low` before any default-effort work, because effort is per generator *process* so packing never mixes the two; a partly tagged slice is narrowed into two slices, one per effort, each re-rendering its own run message. The override travels the same route as the job-level knob — `generatorEnv` sets `MCM_WIKI_REASONING_EFFORT` for that one child process and the usage tap writes `reasoning_effort` onto the Fireworks request bodies — and it is applied only when no explicit effort governs the run and the provider supports `low`.

An explicit reasoning effort — the `reasoning-effort` dispatch input or the `MCM_WIKI_REASONING_EFFORT` repository variable — governs the whole run and the existing tags are merely kept for later (a fresh deadline stop still records a tag, it just does not change what this run sends), and a provider that takes no reasoning effort (`anthropic`) ignores the tags and keeps them; either way the escalation split is skipped rather than applied.

A tag clears when its page lands — including a page that landed inside a part that failed, because tags are per page and not per invocation; a page of a failed part that did land is cleared rather than tagged, which is why the verifier reports the failed *pages* individually. A repeat failure at low increments `failuresAtLow` and the run logs `escalated to low and still failing (N): area/page — consider parking it`; nothing is parked automatically, and since feature 082 parking is a recorded `parked` entry in the same run record rather than a marker trick, made in a reviewed PR and removing the backlog slice AND the `escalations` entry in the same commit. An orphan tag for a page that is neither queued nor present is dropped by the next run, while one for a page that still exists is kept and does nothing until the page is planned again.

The evidence that `low` lands a slow page is one success on one page (078 research R14): `sast-scanning` failed twice at default effort — one deadline stop and one worker exit — landed once at `low`, and a later `low` run on the same page exited its worker again. Escalation therefore guarantees that the retry happens and that a repeat failure is visible; it does not guarantee the page lands.

Each invocation's effort and deadline-stop status are recorded per invocation rather than only per run: `lastRunInvocations` lists every invocation with its `pages`, `effort`, `deadlineStop`, `estCostUsd` and `rateLimited`, and `lastRunUsage.reasoningEffort` reads `mixed` when invocations differ, because naming the first invocation's effort would misattribute the whole run's tokens to it.

A run that finds nothing to document is free and still advances the marker: with an empty plan the record's `coveredCommit` moves to the planned base commit with `lastOutcome: nothing-to-do` and no model is invoked, so the next run over the same tree is free too — but a `--dry-run` persists nothing, so asking what the run would do never certifies the range as covered.

After an ordinary failure, each failed page's page and `.claims` sidecar are restored to their committed bytes and its `.page-manifest.json` entry to its pre-invocation value — all three or none, so V16 still compares a page with its own sidecar — because the proposal stages the whole working tree and otherwise the failed page's bytes would ride along on the proposal of the pages that landed (item #685, measured on #684 / run 4801, where openwiki's restore path had rewritten a page without its `verified:` block and re-hashed its sidecar to match); a page or sidecar already dirty before the invocation, an untracked new page, and anything written outside the requested pages are left alone and can still appear on a proposal.

A failed attempt whose calls were at least half HTTP 429 is recognised from the usage tap's per-call `status` (never the generator's text) and the retry waits 60 s, or 120 s before a third attempt, but only while the retry would still start inside the 4-minute time budget and leave the generator its 5-minute minimum before the job deadline — otherwise it is not retried; an attempt that produced nothing without a 429 still retries immediately, and either way the rate limit is named in the log and as `rateLimited: {attempts, calls}` on the invocation in `lastRunInvocations` (item #683, run 4798).

`node scripts/wiki-maintain.mjs --claims-audit` is a second free, offline, keyless mode (`--json` for machines) that runs openwiki's own `RepositoryEvidenceResolver`, loaded from the install the `openwiki` binary on `PATH` belongs to (exit 2 when there is none), over every sidecar under `openwiki/.claims/` whose page exists; it lists the pages openwiki's claims preflight will force into the next run — a full paid regeneration whatever the plan requested (item #707, matched against run 4972) — and marks a page whose only issues are churn citations (a lockfile, a CD digest pin, a rotating allowlist line) as avoidable, since `openwiki/INSTRUCTIONS.md` §9 forbids citing those.

When a slice's only violation not attributable to a page is the conformance gate, the failed pages are restored first (page, `.claims` sidecar and `.page-manifest.json` entry together, the same triple as item #685) and the slice is judged again; if the bundle is then conformant the break was theirs alone and the pages that landed are proposed (run 5104, 2026-10-11, where one of 15 workers died mid-edit on repeated HTTP 412s and its uncertified V16 bytes would have discarded the other 13, ~$2.66). Since run 5145 a V16 break that names a requested page is itself attributable, so that page is restored, counted as failed and carried forward while the submitted pages beside it are proposed. A policy violation, or a break the restore does not repair, still fails the whole invocation.

Under the page-attributable condition (failure attributable to requested pages, conformance V16 included and policy clean), a page the run wrote but never requested — chiefly a stale-Claims reconciliation openwiki forced in (item #707) — is reported as `forcedPages`, counted as written and proposed, and the proposal body lists it as proposed anyway; after a deadline stop only a forced page whose worker submitted before the stop still qualifies, because `revertUnrequested` has put every other unrequested path back.

The CI runner has no generator baked in, so the wiki-maintain job installs one from a committed lockfile rather than resolving fresh (item #704): `tools/openwiki-generator/` is its own pnpm workspace root holding exact pins for `openwiki` 0.7.1 and its `mermaid`/`jsdom` peers plus a `pnpm-lock.yaml`, the job runs `pnpm --dir tools/openwiki-generator install --frozen-lockfile`, puts that tree's `node_modules/.bin` on `PATH`, and its verify step fails unless `command -v openwiki` resolves there — replacing an `npm install -g openwiki@0.7.1 mermaid jsdom` that pinned only `openwiki` and resolved its whole transitive tree at run time (run 4950, 2026-10-09, died 404-ing on a two-minute-old `openai@7.32.0`).

`tools/openwiki-generator/pnpm-workspace.yaml` sets `minimumReleaseAge: 4320` (three days, Renovate's catch-all) with deliberately no `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` list, and pnpm enforces it twice — at resolve time, so a lockfile regeneration cannot pick a transitive younger than the window (the item #271 gap at the root), and at install time, where a frozen install fails `ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION` rather than install a locked entry inside it; `better-sqlite3` is the one package allowed to run an install script (`allowBuilds`), because openwiki's LangGraph checkpointer loads its native binding at runtime.

Since item #719 each per-call usage line from `scripts/wiki-usage-tap.mjs` also carries the page a worker owns, the response's finish reason (from a fixed set, else `other`), the names of the tools called and how many of their arguments do not parse as JSON — still no prompt, response, argument or error text — and for every page that did not land the run prints that worker's trail to the job log, which tells a truncated turn (`length`), a turn that simply stopped (`stop` with no tool call) and a malformed tool call (`✗args`) apart.

Since feature 082 every plan also looks for **drift** — concepts whose cited source was committed after the page's stamp — using the same comparison as the OKF gate's V12 warning (`scripts/openwiki-drift.mjs`, one definition imported by the gate, the planner and the verifier), bounded to `DRIFT_PAGES_PER_RUN` (2) pages per run, oldest stamp first, and only from the page budget left after change-driven and backlog work so drift cannot starve either; drift beyond the bound is reported, never written to the backlog, a page whose `resource` names a directory is reported unplannable rather than regenerated, `--plan` prints the four groups before anything else, and V12 itself stays a warning that never affects the exit code.

A page that cannot currently be regenerated is **parked** with an entry under `parked` in `openwiki/.maintenance-state.json`, keyed `area/page` and carrying `item`, `since` and `reason`; a parked page is planned by nothing — not by drift, not by a new change to its source, and not from the backlog — `--plan` lists it with its item on every run and reports an entry whose page no longer exists as orphaned, unparking is removing the entry in the change expected to let the page land, and `writeRunRecord` refuses a malformed entry. Until feature 082 parking meant advancing `coveredCommit` past the page's source change and dropping the page from the backlog, which recorded nothing.

The run record's fields are shape-checked before they reach disk: `writeRunRecord` refuses a `parked` entry that is not `{item, since, reason}`, a `lastOutcome` outside `nothing-to-do | completed | failed`, an `escalations` entry whose `effort` is not a string or whose `failuresAtLow` is not a non-negative integer, a non-array `backlog` or `lastRunInvocations`, and a `coveredCommit` that is neither a string nor null — so an invalid record never lands and a corrupt one is a hard read error rather than a silent default.

The `wiki-update` target's `OPENWIKI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=16384` is a floor that a provider row may raise and never lower: since item #719 (PR #732) the `fireworks` row sets `maxOutputTokens` 65536, because DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reasons inside its output budget and dispatch 5115 (2026-10-11) ended this page's worker on both attempts at exactly 16384 output tokens with `finish: length` before the tool call that writes the page; the `anthropic` row deliberately has no raise, because the Anthropic TypeScript SDK refuses a non-streaming request whose `max_tokens` implies more than ten minutes (about 21k), so a higher global cap could break that provider outright. The launcher raises `OPENWIKI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` to the row's value unless an explicit operator value is already at least that high, and output tokens are billed only when generated.

openwiki 0.7.1 finalizes a page's Claims on `submit_page`, so a worker stopped at the deadline or killed mid-edit leaves a requested page whose bytes its Claims sidecar no longer certifies — a V16 break — while the page's stamp is fresh, which makes it neither missing nor stale and invisible to the other checks. Since push run 5145 (2026-10-11), where `projects/sast.md` was that page and five submitted pages including `runbooks/wiki-maintenance.md` were discarded with it, V16 naming the page makes the failure attributable to it: it is restored to its committed bytes (the same page/sidecar/manifest triple as #685), counted as failed and carried forward even when its committed bytes are current, and the pages that landed are proposed.

Two distinct mechanisms keep churn out of Claims evidence, and they are not the same one. The repository-root `.openwikiignore` lists the paths openwiki may never read or cite at all; the operator's 2026-10-12 change (item #739) added `**/pnpm-lock.yaml` and `security/sast/allowlist.yaml` — a lockfile changes on every dependency bump and the SAST allowlist rotates entries weekly — beside the CD promotion files every deploy rewrites (`**/.env.deploy`, measured 36 times in September 2026, item #525/#613). Adding a path there while any `.claims` sidecar still cites it crashes openwiki's Claims preflight (`EvidenceResourceError`, measured), so the citing pages must be uncovered in the same change; a guard reads the real ignore file and every real sidecar so that state cannot be committed. Separately, `--claims-audit`'s **avoidable** label comes from `churnReason()` in `scripts/wiki-claims-audit.mjs`, which applies its own fixed rules (a lockfile by basename, a `.env.deploy` digest pin, a line-addressed `allowlist.yaml` entry, or a cited range holding an `@sha256:` digest) and never reads the ignore file — so a whole-file allowlist citation is ignored but is not churn, and a Dockerfile digest pin is churn but is not ignored. Either way the fix for a churn citation is to cite the manifest, policy or runbook section that states the fact.

`openwiki/.maintenance-state.json`, `.page-manifest.json`, `.last-update.json`, `.run.json` (the generator's own in-progress run) and the `.claims/` sidecars are live state — the next run rewrites them — so a page must describe what their fields mean and where to read them, never copy a current backlog, `escalations` entry, `lastOutcome`, cost or call count into the prose (openwiki/INSTRUCTIONS.md §10): a copied value is wrong by the next run and a page that quotes it looks authoritative while it is stale. Proposal #737 published exactly such a `lastOutcome`/`failuresAtLow`/cost snapshot in `runbooks/wiki-maintenance.md`, already false when proposed. A measured value that explains why a rule exists is different: it belongs in the source runbook, dated and with its run number, and the page cites it from there.

A `parked` entry in the run record is not always a page whose worker keeps failing: a page whose `resource` names a directory cannot be regenerated durably, because any commit anywhere under that directory re-flags the page as drift (V12), so such a page is parked rather than paid for (item #739, which parked `process/spec-driven-development.md`, whose `resource` is `specs/`).

Overlapping maintenance runs are handled by three mechanisms (#748): the job moves to the current tip of `main` after the debounce and `--execute` stops before any paid generation with exit 0 when the checkout's run record is behind the remote's, while the self-trigger skip decision still reads the event commit; the record commit is a three-way merge (`--merge-record --base --ours --theirs`) in which a field only one side changed takes that side's value, `escalations`, `parked` and the backlog merge per page, the marker never moves backwards, and two different proposal pointers are a refused conflict committed as nothing; and a packed multi-area entry already in a committed backlog is split back into its per-area slices so it is not planned as a new area to create.

A drifted page the open proposal already holds fresh is skipped rather than planned again (#748): the planner reads each drift candidate from the proposal branch, `--plan` lists it as `on the open proposal`, and only drift is skipped — work queued by a source change or by a failure is always planned, because freshness compares commit dates and a merged branch keeps its commit's own earlier date.

The page states the canonical-home rule only as a summary with a pointer, not as a restatement of the brief: a durable learning goes to the canonical home of its subject — into the cited source when the covering concept carries a `resource` (a derived summary), and into the concept itself when it carries none (authoritative) — and the page defers to `openwiki/INSTRUCTIONS.md` §7 and to the process page's 'Where a new learning goes' for the full rule, the rejected grow-then-trim alternative and the G11/G12 enforcement.
